problem: Prior zero-shot LLM navigation agents (NavGPT, MapGPT) use text-only LLMs plus a separate image-to-text captioner, which produces instruction-agnostic, misleading descriptions and creates an image-text gap. They also rely on costly GPT-4 with long histories.
motivation: Multi-modal LLMs can take images directly, but images use up the token quota, so visual history cannot fit. They also handle spatial relations poorly (for example, up vs. down stairs). A cheap, free-API multi-modal agent needs a way to avoid carrying history and to handle different instruction sub-types.
key_idea: Use Gemini-Pro-Vision directly on neighbor images, and repeatedly shrink the instruction to its unfinished remainder, so each query only decides the first step and needs no history.
insight: Rewriting the instruction as the not-yet-completed remainder replaces visual history and keeps prompts short. Table 5 shows that subtask-specific prompts matter: adding the directional and stair prompts raises SR from 35.1 to 36.2 and then 39.7. Table 3 shows that termination check and probe raise SR (37.3 to 38.0 to 39.7) but lengthen paths (TL 11.66 to 40.33) and cut SPL (32.1 to 13.3). The step-wise analysis shows that residual errors come from the LLM being unable to separate nearby, similarly-directed neighbors.
method: Prompt manager: extracts the first step of the instruction, classifies it as regular, directional or stair-related, and selects the matching neighbor-selection prompt

Main query: the multi-modal LLM sees images of each neighbor viewpoint (view toward that neighbor) and picks one to move to, or stops; it considers only the first step of the current instruction and uses no history

Instruction reduction: given the before and after observations, extracted landmarks and directions, and direction/stair info, the LLM compares the images and writes the remaining instruction; 'stop' means finished

Termination check and selection: from step tc=6, each viewpoint's panorama is queried (Yes/No/Unknown); Yes-candidates are stored, and at the end a selection prompt picks the best one from the earlier observations looking toward each candidate

Backtracking: keeps a history trajectory and a navigation trajectory; if there are no termination candidates and the depth limit (Mdepth=10) is reached or all neighbors are dead ends, it returns to the previous viewpoint and restores the earlier instruction (Mstep=20)
Probe: if the chosen neighbor and its nearest neighbor differ by less than an angle threshold, the agent visits both and a probe prompt picks between the two new views

setting.backbone: Gemini-Pro-Vision (frozen, multi-modal queries) + Gemini-Pro (frozen, text-only queries)
setting.observation: panoramic RGB from the Matterport3D discrete nav-graph; per-neighbor view images and panoramas used for termination checks
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints (select a neighbor, stop, or backtrack)

numbers.extra: probe and termination check; long paths (TL 40.33); tc=6, Mstep=20, Mdepth=10

numbers_note: The abstract's '5.7% SR' is computed against NavGPT (34 SR) on R2R. The paper says it uses the 783 trajectories in the 11 val-unseen environments, yet elsewhere mentions 2349 instructions. Both are treated as the full split.
results: On R2R val-unseen, the full model reaches SR 39.7, NE 5.79 and OSR 55.7 versus NavGPT's 34 SR, 6.46 NE and 42 OSR, but SPL falls to 13.3 because of very long paths. Without probe and termination, SR is 37.3 and SPL 32.1 (NavGPT 29). On REVERIE the full model gets SR 22.0 versus NavGPT's 19.2, and the lighter variant gets SPL 16.9 versus 14.6. It remains far below trained methods such as DuET.
limitations: Probe and termination checks make the agent move back and forth, so TL is 40.33 on R2R and SPL is very low.
Prompts are handcrafted per subtask type, and the LLM cannot distinguish small angular differences between nearby neighbors.
Still far below supervised methods (DuET SR 72 on R2R), and the evaluation covers only discrete R2R and REVERIE, with no real-robot tests.
